per_source: The Catholic World, Vol. 04, October, 1866 to March, 1867
per_quote: We alter not, we control not by our machinery the forces of nature, and all the advantage we have obtained is in conforming to them, and in suffering them, according to their own laws, or laws which we have not imposed on them, to operate for us.
per_position: Does not weaken; only reason is an irrelevant claim that machines cannot remove clouds.

position: Does not weaken; relying on machines frees attention to concentrate on one's work.
quote: He need not, for instance, grind his corn in a hand-quern; a little trickle of water, a wheel, and a few simple contrivances will do it all perfectly well, and leave him free to smoke his pipe and think, or to carve the handle of his knife.
per_source: The Continental Monthly, Vol. 5, No. 3,  March, 1864
per_quote: The former causes had a mechanical tendency in that they lessened the mental strength, for all volition must have its foundation in thought; but this has the same tendency, inasmuch as it increases the objects of thought beyond the power of the mind to satisfy the demand.
per_position: Does not weaken: relying on machines frees attention to concentrate on one's work.

position: Depends: dependence is good, abuse bad; we must not become their slaves.
quote: This fact precludes us from proposing the complete annihilation of machinery, but surely it indicates that we should destroy as many of them as we can possibly dispense with, lest they should tyrannise over us even more completely.
per_source: The Catholic World, Vol. 14, October 1871-March 1872
per_quote: They also tend to convert the independent laborer into a workman at wages, and the freeman into the slave of machinery, to enrich a few railway presidents and directors, and stock-jobbers.
per_position: Depends: dependence is good, abuse bad; indispensable but must not enslave us.

position: Depends: inventive capacity may shrink, but capacity to use machines grows.
quote: The increase in the reward of labor and capital would still further stimulate invention and hasten the adoption of improved processes, and these would truly appear, what in themselves they really are—an unmixed good.
per_position: Depends; inventive capacity may shrink, but capacity to use machines grows.

position: Weakens; outsourcing faculties to the Machine atrophies body, mind, and will.
quote: He feared that the removal of the present pressure might cause a degeneracy of the human race, and indeed that the whole body might become purely rudimentary, the man himself being nothing but soul and mechanism, an intelligent but passionless principle of mechanical action.

position: Depends: machines let the mind drift, but training keeps the machine a servant.
quote: He is the slave to machinery; the new machine _must_ be invented, and when invented he _must_—I will not say use it, but be used by it, whether he likes it or not.
per_source: The Catholic World, Vol. 19, April 1874‐September 1874
per_quote: “The primary principle of education is the determination of the pupil to self‐activity—the doing nothing for him which he is able to do for himself.”
per_position: Depends: machines let the mind drift, but a trained mind keeps control.

position: None; says the two views are antagonistic, gives no reason.
per_position: None: fragment about antagonistic views; no verdict, no reason.

position: Does not weaken; technology frees cognitive resources for higher-order skills.
quote: He need not, for instance, grind his corn in a hand-quern; a little trickle of water, a wheel, and a few simple contrivances will do it all perfectly well, and leave him free to smoke his pipe and think, or to carve the handle of his knife.
per_source: Graham's Magazine, Vol. XL, No. 6, June 1852
per_quote: It is little to say this—yet this is something; for it is the first step toward making those who do govern the land, fit to govern it—namely, the people—toward enabling them to judge, unlike the constituents of best European representative governments, not of men only, but, mediately, of measures; toward giving them to judge and learn for themselves, from the actual progress of recorded events, daily occuring, something of the policy of foreign nations, something of the interest of their own country; lastly, toward rendering the permanent establishment of a falsehood, or the long suppression of the truth, an impossibility.
per_position: Does not weaken; machines free cognition for higher-order work, as the printing press did.

position: Weakens; machines substitute less intelligent workers for more intelligent ones.
source: Babbage, On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures (1832)
quote: On the other hand, although new machinery causes an increased demand for skill in those who make and repair it, and in those who first superintend its use; yet there are other cases in which it enables children and inferior workmen to execute work that previously required greater skill.

position: Does not weaken with correct use; only useless mental lumber suffers. No coherent reason.
quote: In fact, machines are to be regarded as the mode of development by which human organism is now especially advancing, every past invention being an addition to the resources of the human body.
per_source: The Atlantic Monthly, Volume 01, No. 01, November, 1857
per_quote: But the calculating power alone should seem to be the least human of qualities, and to have the smallest amount of reason in it; since a machine can be made to do the work of three or four calculators, and better than any one of them.
per_position: Does not weaken: correct use only sheds useless mental lumber.

position: Weakens; circular claim that machines are used only where capacities are weak.
quote: A few miserable individuals might linger, but even these in a year or two would become worse than monkeys.
per_position: Weakens, via looping circular reasoning; no coherent reason given.

position: Weakens; mechanical work makes man automatic, developing the machine rather than manhood.
source: Ruskin, The Stones of Venice, vol. 2 (1853)
quote: If you will have that precision out of them, and make their fingers measure degrees like cog-wheels, and their arms strike curves like compasses, you must unhumanize them.

position: Weakens; unexercised skills atrophy, leaving people dependent if technology fails.
quote: He is at the mercy of the seeing-engine for these things, and is powerless unless he tack it on to his own identity, and make it part and parcel of himself.
per_source: The Continental Monthly, Vol. 5, No. 3,  March, 1864
per_quote: The question whether our social state is becoming mechanical, losing personal thought and volition, is of great and vital importance, on account of the terrible major premise that lies beneath.
per_position: Weakens: disused skills atrophy, creating dependence if technology fails.

position: Depends on use; cognition is plastic and shifts to higher-order tasks.
quote: That, so far, is unmixed gain in the use of a machine—always, mind you, supposing equality of condition among men; no art is lost, leisure or time for more pleasurable work is gained.
per_source: Graham's Magazine, Vol. XLI, No. 2, August 1852
per_quote: In savage life, invention flags—its exercise is rare; but it is frequent in a highly civilized condition.
per_position: Does not weaken inherently: cognition adapts; outcome depends on use.

position: Does not weaken (strengthens); machines take over hand work and civilization depends on them.
quote: In the new era the stress falls rather more decidedly on general intelligence and information, as contrasted with detail mastery of the minutiæ of a trade; so that familiarity with the commonplace technological knowledge of the time is rather more imperative a requirement under the machine technology than under that of handicraft.
per_position: Does not weaken: machines doing handwork strengthen human capacities.

position: Does not weaken overall; physical strength atrophies but intellect and cooperation expand.
quote: He feared that the removal of the present pressure might cause a degeneracy of the human race, and indeed that the whole body might become purely rudimentary, the man himself being nothing but soul and mechanism, an intelligent but passionless principle of mechanical action.
per_source: The Popular Science Monthly, October, 1900
per_quote: If, then, man by his power of mental energy converts the original and crude forces with which the earth is endowed into new forms, and by giving them new direction increases his power of production of the means of his own subsistence and enjoyment of life, _does it not follow that creation is a continuous procession in which man is a factor_?
per_position: Does not weaken overall: lost physical traits are offset by expanded intellect.

position: Does not weaken; racial comparison of Italians and Eastern peoples.
per_source: The Chautauquan, Vol. 05, April 1885
per_quote: Why should we, indeed, when we remember that both are alike untaught in the arts and sciences which form the basis of mechanical invention?
per_position: Does not weaken: machine-using West (Italians) advanced intellectually; East did not.

position: Does not weaken overall; physical skills atrophy but cognitive faculties are amplified.
quote: He feared that the removal of the present pressure might cause a degeneracy of the human race, and indeed that the whole body might become purely rudimentary, the man himself being nothing but soul and mechanism, an intelligent but passionless principle of mechanical action.
per_source: Appletons' Popular Science Monthly, January 1899
per_quote: Our sense organs are thus indefinitely multiplied and extended by such extra-organic sense organs as the microscope, telescope, resonator, telephone, telegraph, thermometer, etc.
per_position: Depends: some physical skills atrophy, but technology reallocates energy to amplified cognitive capacities.

position: Does not weaken; automating mundane tasks frees the mind for higher thinking.
quote: He need not, for instance, grind his corn in a hand-quern; a little trickle of water, a wheel, and a few simple contrivances will do it all perfectly well, and leave him free to smoke his pipe and think, or to carve the handle of his knife.

position: Does not weaken; machines redirect capacities to production for common use.
source: Babbage, On the Economy of Machinery and Manufactures (1832)
quote: Frequently the new labour requires, at its commencement, a higher degree of skill than the old; and, unfortunately, the class of persons driven out of the old employment are not always qualified for the new one; so that a certain interval must elapse before the whole of their labour is wanted.
per_position: Does not weaken: capacities are redirected to production for all, not reduced.
